en: Ādyanātha: *Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā* Oṃ. Salutation to Śaṅkara, the unsurpassed light.
Śiva is the single, solid mass of light consisting of the uncontrived self-awareness of "I."
By means of power, whose nature is reflective awareness and which is non-different from one's own self.
Manifesting the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth as his own body,
the Lord, who delights in the great drama of the fivefold cosmic acts, sports.
The two bodies, Viśvaviśva and Śarīra, possess distinct meanings and functional purposes;
yet there is no ontological difference whatsoever between Viśvaviśva and Viśvavapuḥ.
If there were a difference [between the Self and the world], how could the world exist as distinct from existence (sattā) and manifestation (sphurattā)?
For it would not exist unless it were connected to existence and manifestation, nor would it have the appearance of existence.

What [relation] could there be between the non-existent and the existent? This very relation is asserted [by you], yet a relation easily obtained through the acquisition of its own nature does not belong to a non-entity. (Aprp 5)
When no connection with a form has been apprehended by those two, nothing at all is disregarded;
if there were disregard, this [cognition] would have no state whatsoever.
By its very nature, radiance and existence are not subject to destruction;
if destruction were not admitted, even insentience would be excluded.
Therefore, since there is no other state of being, consciousness alone remains;
and the oneness of consciousness with the existent, which was the subject under discussion, never ceases at any time.
In the Light, existence is not from another; it is the sole radiance of absolute sovereignty.
This is the power of Śambhu, who transcends the universe, whose nature is yet delimited. 9. Aprp.
Whatever is of the nature of light has all become pure darkness;
and whatever little of this world remains, it does not exceed that light. (Aprp 10)
"This has been reached by reflecting upon the path"—this is the ultimate cognition;
here, the single cognition consisting of the uniformity of appearances is the witness. (Aprp 11)
Of what use are those wretched means of knowledge, whose very selves are animated by consciousness?
For the sun-like light does not depend upon the illumination of a lamp. (Aprp 12)
Let this principle of consciousness (dhītattva), purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta), be examined;
yet, even within its mirror-like, stainless expanse, not everything is manifested.
Thus, everything consists of consciousness through the thirty-sixfold division of principles (*tattva*);
first is the pure principle, which is fivefold and beyond darkness (*tamas*).
Śiva, Śakti, Sadākhya, Īśa, and Vidya—thus [the system] is divided;
yet it was fashioned by Śiva as consisting of the phonemes from 'a' (akṣa) up to 'kṣa' (śānta).
Bondage is said to consist of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*;
it is preceded by *māyā* and consists of the letters beginning with *va* and ending with *kṣa*. (Aprp 16)
The Puruṣa, Śakti, mind, intellect, and the pentad beginning with ego; the pentad beginning with the ear, the pentad beginning with *ṭa*, and the pentad beginning with speech. (Aprp 17)

The five subtle elements (tanmātras), the letters beginning with 'a', and the five [gross elements] beginning with space are known as the Śiva-tattva of the all-pervading Lord, which is His first vibration when desiring to emit [the universe]. (Aprp 18)
That very desire, unfading, manifesting the principle of power (śaktitattva), remains covering the universe—which was indicated by its own will—through the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā). 19.
That very [consciousness] is the *tattva* called Sādākhya, intent upon bestowing grace upon all;
that same [consciousness], perceiving the universe as "this" (*idantayā*), becomes the *tattva* of Īśvara.
The knowledge that "this-ness" and "I-ness" are one is called *vidyā*; the notion of duality regarding objects that are like one's own limbs is the principle of *māyā*. (Aprp 21)
Śiva, when contracted by the grasp of *māyā*, is called the *puruṣatattva*;
for he alone is seen as the transmigrating soul (*jīva*), the enjoyer. (Aprp 22)
Knowledge, agency, fullness, and eternity are the powers of the Other;
through their contraction, [the Self] is considered contracted by way of having *kalā* and the other [categories] as its nature. (Aprp 23)
Māyā is essentially the principle called *kalā*, which is the cause of limited agency;
*kāla* (time) effects limitation, and *niyati* (fate) is likewise this very same thing for me. (Aprp 24)
The rule that "nothing else is to be done" is the form of restraint;
primordial nature (prakṛti) is the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), the birthplace of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra) and the rest. (Aprp 25)
The ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is the cause of the cognition "I" and "this is mine";
the intellect (buddhi) is the cause of determination (adhyavasāya), which consists of ascertainment.
The mind is declared to be the seed of conceptualization and discursive thought;
and from speech and so forth, as well as sound and so forth, arise speech, hearing, and the rest. (Aprp 27)
The five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) are to be understood as the cause of hearing and the other [sensory capacities];
the five gross elements (bhūta-pañcaka), beginning with space, are the cause of space and the other [objective domains]. (Aprp 28)
In the pure [reality] consisting of the power that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāparā), there is the pentad beginning with Vidyā;
that which is other than this is the non-supreme power (aparā)—this is declared to be the reality (tattva). (Aprp 29)
This goddess is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), containing within her womb both the pure and impure paths;
it is she into whom the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth are dissolved when they reach their cause.
Then the All-pervasive Lord emits the mere causes externally;
in the supreme will, the unfolding, and the bliss, there is the teaching on the state of being "less" (ūnatā).

The existence of the powers of action, will, and knowledge constitutes the sixfold [reality]. Mounted within the interior of will and sovereignty, it consists of the world in both its manifest and unmanifest forms. (Aprp 32)
*COMM: Regarding the three verses beginning with "anuttara," it appears there is a textual corruption due to an inconsistency in meaning.
[The corrected reading is: "The four subsequent phonemes, whose nature is the neuter (*ṣaṇḍa*), are impelled;
the power of supreme bliss (*anuttarānanda-śakti*) arises from the triangle through its connection with the circular movement. (Aprp 33)

In the same way, through the yoga of Unmanā, the manifest form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is described as the trident (triśūla), which devours duality, arising from the union of the three powers.
But when they are mutually contradictory regarding their effects, this nature of theirs can in no way be accepted as valid. (Aprp 35)
The Bindu is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the object of knowledge; it is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and this is emission (*sarga*).
Thus, the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), whose form consists of the sixteen digits (*kalā*), reigns supreme.
By means of Māyā, there are fifteen lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad),
for the sake of maintaining existence as the sun and moon move within one's own heart.
Just as the primordial elements of creation are known to have the nature of non-discrimination, so too this Goddess Mātṛkā exists in two ways, through her essence as both seed and womb. (Aprp 38)
The body of the Śṛṅgāṭa is eternally active and is the birthplace of the universe;
its heart is the seed, which is that supreme light, the essence within it.
Just as a tree exists within a banyan seed, so too is the entire world contained herein;
when investigated, this world does not exist apart from its cause.
"In the investigation of reality, the essence of jars and the like is nothing other than clay and so forth"—thus say the final words of the scriptures, which speak the truth of reality. (Aprp 41)
Because of the certainty that "in the beginning all this was indeed Being," this world appears as illusion within this seed which denotes existence. (Aprp 42)
This [reality] remains as that in which the forms of causal conditions have been dissolved;
from it arise Jñāna, Kriyā, Sāra, Vidyeśvara, and Sadāśiva. (Aprp 43)
They dissolve into the trident of power (śaktitriśūla), which consists of fourteen kalās;
since everything is dissolved within that whose form is the upward and downward emanation, there is nothing beyond this.
In this way, everything contracted gradually within the supreme consciousness;
or rather, [it is dissolved] anywhere at all within the stainless state that transcends the mind.
She dissolves into that very nature—the Great Mantra which is the self of the universe and the domain beyond the conflict of the thirty-six principles. (Aprp 46)
And when his abode has been kindled by someone for whatever reason, he who offers all this oblation is not afflicted by poverty. (Aprp 47)
The universe, consisting of five times five and manifested through the fivefold vibration,
is contracted by means of reflective awareness into the solitary, universal vibration.
Bringing about the dissolution of this "thisness" which stands as its opposite, I,
intent upon supreme valor, enjoy my own nature which removes all inauspiciousness.
Thus, the great canvas, variegated by the manifestation of the Great Power, unfolds with a body that extends through the thirty-six possible divisions of the world.
Victorious is the supreme, unsurpassed Consciousness, whose form is manifold vibration; O people who reflect upon this, why do you not realize that it is the unfolding of your own essential nature?

Thus ends the *Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā* composed by the illustrious Ādinātha. This has been published by Mukundarāma, who resides under the patronage of the King of Kashmir; may it be for the joy of the virtuous and be offered to Śiva. 1. Aprp_*1.
